transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

I feel like I’m constantly trying to make up for eating too much, and it’s taking over how I plan my days. My primary care doctor actually suggested I come in for a psychiatric evaluation after I talked to him about how much I've been struggling with this lately.
Have you been using methods like vomiting, laxatives, or excessive exercise to try to compensate for eating?

Yes, I actually do both, and it's honestly exhausting and embarrassing to admit. Some nights after overeating, I'll force myself to throw up because I just can't stand the thought of all that food turning into weight. Other days, I try to punish myself by skipping breakfast and lunch, and forcing myself to run extra laps after soccer practice even when I'm wiped out from a 10-hour shift at the shop.
Can you tell me more about the frequency of these behaviors, specifically how often you engage in self-induced vomiting versus the other methods like excessive exercise or restrictive eating?

For the last few months, it's been a weekly cycle where I do this about once or twice a week. On some of those nights, I'll end up making myself throw up, while other times I try to "cancel it out" by skipping breakfast and lunch and forcing myself to run extra laps.
Do you have a significant fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, which drives your behaviors to compensate for eating?

Yes, I absolutely freak out about gaining weight, and it's what drives all of this. I constantly check the scale at the shop and panic if I'm even a pound heavier, worrying that every slice of pizza is going straight to my gut. That fear is exactly why I'll skip meals, run until I'm exhausted, or make myself throw up just to stop the food from turning into weight.

Do you also experience distressing thoughts or beliefs about your body shape or weight, beyond just the fear of gaining weight, such as feeling that your self-worth is heavily influenced by your weight or body shape?

Yes, I really struggle with that. When I look in the mirror, I don't see a guy who passed his certs and keeps trucks running; I just see a soft belly and love handles. It makes me feel like a complete failure, especially compared to the younger techs at the shop who are always posting their gym pics.

Can you tell me if your fear of gaining weight and your self-worth being heavily influenced by your weight or body shape occur even when you're at a normal weight or only when you've recently overeaten?

I'm not entirely sure how to break it down that way, to be honest. But those feelings of panic about my weight and feeling like a failure when I look in the mirror seem to be there constantly lately, rather than just right after a heavy night of eating.
Have you experienced any changes in your menstrual cycle, such as irregular periods or amenorrhea, which is the absence of menstruation, as a result of your weight and eating habits?
Actually, I'm a guy, so I don't have a menstrual cycle. But the physical strain of everything else has definitely been wearing me down in other ways.

Given that you're a male and the behaviors and fears you've described, can you tell me if you've experienced any significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning as a result of your eating habits and fear of gaining weight?

It's definitely taken a massive toll on my life. I've been turning down weekend hikes and playing worse at soccer because I'm either completely exhausted from skipping meals or sore from pushing myself too hard. Even at work, I find myself constantly distracted by planning how to "fix" what I ate instead of focusing on the trucks.
Do you have a persistent and intrusive preoccupation with a specific aspect of your appearance, such as a perceived flaw or defect, that is not solely related to your weight or body shape?
No, I don't really have concerns about other specific features of my appearance like that. My worries are pretty much entirely focused on my weight, my belly, and my overall body shape.
